content: There is no universally agreed-upon standard for what constitutes a normal serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] level. A threshold of 12 ng/mL (30 nmol/L) has been proposed by some experts. In reality, the majority of the population (approximately 97.5%) requires a serum 25(OH)D level of 20 ng/mL or less to meet their physiological needs. Furthermore, based on the Estimated Average Requirement (EAR), about half of the population has a requirement of 16 ng/mL (40 nmol/L) or less. Previous guidelines have suggested that serum 25(OH)D levels at or below 20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L) fall within the deficient range. One method of defining deficiency involves identifying the serum 25(OH)D level at which parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion plateaus. This threshold may be as low as 12 ng/mL (30 nmol/L) or as high as 30 ng/mL (75 nmol/L), depending on the criteria used. The Institute of Medicine (IOM) provides the following classifications for serum 25(OH)D levels: Levels above 20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L): Practically all individuals are sufficient. Levels between 12-20 ng/mL (30-50 nmol/L): Some, but not all, individuals are potentially at risk for inadequacy. Levels below 12 ng/mL (30 nmol/L): Individuals are at risk of deficiency.
